text: An AI visibility score condenses four signals into a single 0-100 figure: how many relevant questions mention you (query coverage), how prominently you are cited (position-weighted citations), how much of the conversation you own against competitors ( AI share of voice ), and how often you are named without a link (soft mentions). This guide explains what each of the four measures and how to read its movement. It does not reproduce a full composite formula, because MentionOwl, the tool I use as the worked example, does not publish its weighting. You cannot recalculate the headline number independently, and I won't pretend otherwise. What you can do is understand the component signals well enough to see which one moved, explain why, and report it with confidence. Disclosure and scope. MentionOwl is the worked example throughout, and I work with it, so treat product-specific details as vendor descriptions, not industry standards. Where I give general advice, it applies to any tool. There is no standardised, industry-wide AI visibility score: tools sample different platforms, prompts and competitors, and they define visibility differently. A score only means something alongside its methodology. What is an AI visibility score, and why does a single number help? Leadership wants one trend line, and marketing needs the components underneath it to act. A composite serves both audiences, provided you never report it without its parts. On its own it can hide the difference between being mentioned, being cited as a source, being recommended and being described favourably. A score that holds steady at 54 might mean coverage rose while citations fell, and those two situations call for very different responses. Why AI search needs repeated sampling Classic rank tracking gives you a position for a keyword on a given day. AI answers behave differently. They vary by engine, by phrasing and by day, and Google notes that results can differ by platform, location, language, personalisation and measurement date. A single snapshot is a weak basis for conclusions. Repeated sampling gives you many observations of the same question set, and aggregating them (a rolling seven-day average or a weekly median, for instance) shows whether the underlying direction is changing. The aggregation method matters, so ask any vendor how daily runs are combined into the figure you see, or record it yourself. There is also a commercial reason to measure visibility separately from clicks. Pew Research Center analysed the browsing of 900 U.S. adults in March 2025 (68,879 Google searches) and found an AI summary on about 18% of searches. Users clicked a traditional result in 8% of visits when a summary appeared, against 15% when it did not, and only about 1% clicked a link inside the summary ( Pew Research Center, July 2025 ). That describes U.S. Google behaviour, not UK behaviour, and it does not show that any brand's score drives revenue. Gartner has also forecast that traditional search engine volume will fall 25% by 2026 as users move to AI chatbots ( Gartner press release, February 2024 ). It is a forecast, not a measured outcome. The engines and method behind MentionOwl's AI visibility score MentionOwl states that it tracks ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot and Perplexity. It crawls your website, auto-generates the customer questions your pages should answer, and runs them daily against each engine, recording the answer, citations, sentiment and competitor mentions. Covering several engines matters because buyers do not all use the same assistant. Before trusting a figure like this, I would ask the vendor how many prompts sit behind it, how often they are refreshed, which market and language settings are applied, and how runs are aggregated. Any proprietary score is a model. Its value lies in consistent methodology and trend direction, not the absolute number. If the question set, engines, market or weighting change, treat that as a break in the time series, not as ordinary performance movement. How the 0-100 AI visibility score is built: four components The four components combine into one score, but you should review them individually. To be precise about what is and is not public: MentionOwl does not disclose the exact weighting between components, nor every counting rule, so I won't invent them. The definitions below are the ones I use in this guide's worked examples. Where your tool's rules differ, document them in a methodology note. Component What it measures What a rise may mean What a fall may mean Who owns the fix Query coverage Share of tracked questions where your brand appears at all You are surfacing for more buyer questions Lost ground on topics, a stronger competitor page, a model change or a technical barrier Content and SEO, with web development for technical issues Position-weighted citations How often and how prominently your pages are cited as sources; earlier positions count for more Your pages are being cited earlier or more often Thinner or dated pages, weaker structure, or a rival publishing original research Content and PR AI share of voice Your portion of all brand mentions against named competitors You are gaining relative to rivals A competitor gaining, even if your own activity is unchanged Marketing leadership and competitive intelligence Soft mentions Brand references without a citation or link Possibly growing brand familiarity in AI answers Possibly weaker third-party presence PR, reviews and brand The "may mean" wording is deliberate. These are interpretations to test against your own data, not proven causes. I would put this table in your reporting pack as it stands, because it answers "what moved, and whose job is it?" before anyone asks. Query coverage: how often does your brand appear in AI answers? Query coverage is the proportion of tracked questions for which your brand appears in an AI-generated answer. Take an illustrative example: 200 tracked questions, with your brand appearing in 56 answers, so coverage is 56 / 200 = 28%. The numerator is questions with at least one mention, the denominator is all tracked questions, and the sampling unit is the question, not each separate run. The result depends on the question set and on what counts as a mention, so document both. Why the question set matters Questions derived from your own website tend to reflect your own positioning. That is useful, but it can bias the set towards topics you already cover. I recommend validating a generated set against customer research, sales-call questions and independent category queries. A good set spans discovery, comparison and purchase stages, and you should report results by topic or intent as well as in aggregate. This is also why I separate branded from unbranded questions. Suppose, illustratively, that 50 of your 200 questions name your brand and you appear in 45 of them, while you appear in 11 of the other 150. Headline coverage is 56 of 200, or 28%, but unbranded coverage is only 7.3% (11 of 150). Unbranded coverage is a useful indicator of discovery, because it shows whether people who do not yet know you are being introduced to you. It is still just one indicator, and it depends on how representative the unbranded questions are. How engines, markets and technical issues affect query coverage Coverage differs by engine, and one assistant lagging can drag the blended figure down, so review engines separately before drawing conclusions. Market and language matter too. Google's AI features are available in many countries and languages, and the Pew figures above are U.S.-only, so a result from one market should not be generalised to another. For a UK business, that has practical consequences. Specify UK English in prompts ("accountancy software" rather than "accounting software", "trainers" rather than "sneakers"), set a UK location where the tool allows it, and name UK competitors, since a global rival that dominates US answers may barely register in UK ones. Report UK tracking separately from any US tracking, and note regulatory or seasonal context, such as the April tax year, when you interpret a movement. In my experience of reviewing these reports, a coverage shift usually traces back to one of these: New content being crawled, which can lift coverage A competitor publishing a stronger page on the same topic An engine updating its model or search features Technical barriers on your own site Treat these as working hypotheses to check against the data. I am not claiming they rank in that order of likelihood. The link between AI legibility and query coverage Blocked crawlers, unclear structure or broken pages can suppress coverage regardless of content quality. MentionOwl's AI legibility audit runs 16 technical checks to surface such problems, and any technical SEO audit does the same job. Google states that its AI features rely on the same foundational SEO practices as its other Search features and need no special technical optimisation ( Google Search Central ), so in most cases the fix is ordinary good practice: indexable, accessible, genuinely useful pages. Position-weighted citations: why citation order matters A citation is a source your brand's page is credited as in an answer, usually shown as a link or footnote. Position-weighting gives earlier citations more credit than later ones. I treat this as a reporting heuristic, not a proven measure of influence. It is plausible that users give most attention to what they see first, but nobody has established how that plays out across AI engines, and the weights in any model are the publisher's methodological choice. Classic search offers a useful but limited analogy. Backlinko's analysis of 4 million Google search results found the first organic result averaged a 27.6% click-through rate, against 15.8% for the second and 11.0% for the third ( Backlinko ). That shows order shapes attention in traditional search. It does not tell us that AI answers follow the same distribution. An illustrative citation-weighting example The weights below are an example only, not MentionOwl's actual weights: Position 1: 1.0 Position 2: 0.7 Position 3: 0.5 Position 4: 0.35 Position 5: 0.25 Under these example weights, one first-position citation scores 1.0, while two citations in positions four and five together score 0.6. Frequency still counts, since three low-position citations (positions 3, 4 and 5) would total 1.1, but prominence changes the arithmetic considerably. That is why I recommend reporting raw citation counts and the position distribution alongside any weighted figure. Citation frequency versus citation quality Citation frequency and citation quality are different things. Review which of your pages are being cited and which competitor pages win the questions you lose. When citations slip, check four things first: whether a rival's content is fuller than yours, whether your statistics are outdated, whether your structured data is weaker, and whether a competitor has added original research. In my own reviews, pages that earn early citations often have clear answers, original data and authoritative sourcing, but that is an observation from practice, not a finding from controlled research. The practical levers within generative engine optimization are answer-first formatting, original data, clear sourcing and well-structured pages, and all of them help human readers too. AI share of voice and soft mentions AI share of voice is your mentions divided by total mentions of you and your tracked competitors across the same question set. Counting rules change the answer, so define them. In my examples, each brand counts once per answer (repeat mentions within a single answer are not added), and both cited and uncited mentions are included. If you are mentioned in 30 answers and three competitors in 45, 15 and 10, your share is 30 of 100, or 30%. It is a relative measure. It can rise because you appear more often, because competitors appear less, or because the tracked prompts changed, and on its own it does not establish traffic, leads or sales. Why competitor tracking is essential for AI share of voice Your score can fall even when you have done nothing wrong, because a rival gained ground. Without competitor tracking you would see the dip but not the cause. Reporting share of voice as a trend against two or three named competitors, rather than as a standalone percentage, shows leadership whether the market is moving and not only whether you are. What is a soft mention in AI search? A soft mention is your brand named in an answer without a link or formal citation, for example "Brand X is a popular option for…". Definitions vary between tools, and some use "soft" for descriptions that do not name the brand at all, so state your definition in your methodology note. In MentionOwl's model it means named but not linked. Soft mentions may indicate that a model is familiar with your brand, and some practitioners expect them to come before citations as visibility matures. I would treat that progression as a hypothesis to test in your own data, not an established pattern. They carry less weight than a prominent citation, yet a named brand can still shape a buyer's shortlist. Pair AI mentions with sentiment A negative or caveated mention should not be reported as a win. A rising mention count with deteriorating sentiment is a warning, not progress. Record mentions, soft mentions, citations, prominence and sentiment separately, because AI answers vary between runs and blended figures can mask these differences. Why did my AI visibility score drop this week? A diagnostic checklist Work through these steps in order. In my experience they usually isolate the likely cause quickly. Check blended versus single-engine movement. A drop confined to one engine points to that engine, not to your brand. Identify the component that moved most. The table above tells you who owns the fix. Review competitor tracking. Look for new entrants or sudden gains that explain a share-of-voice dip. Look for a model or search-feature update. An engine change can shift every brand at once. Run a technical audit. Rule out crawl blocks, broken pages or structural problems. Compare against the aggregated trend. Use a rolling average over two to four weeks of daily data, not a single reading. Annotate the change. Record the likely cause so leadership gets an explanation and not just a number. What is a good AI visibility score? There is no universal benchmark, and I won't offer numeric thresholds because I have no market data to validate them. Scores are comparable only when the prompt set, platforms, locations and scoring method are aligned, so a good score is relative to your category and competitors. A niche UK business can lead a small category, while the same number may be much harder to reach in a crowded market with well-funded rivals. Instead of bands, I recommend three habits. First, fix the comparison set: benchmark against a stable list of direct competitors on the same questions, platforms and market, and document it. Second, prioritise direction of travel by judging a rolling average over several weeks, not any single reading. Third, set component targets, such as raising unbranded query coverage by a set number of percentage points over a quarter. Also segment results by topic, intent, market and engine. A brand can be strong on informational questions and weak on purchase comparisons, and a single grade would hide that. How to improve your AI visibility score and report it to leadership These actions apply with any tool: Fix technical foundations first. Crawl or indexing barriers can suppress coverage and citations, so rule them out before anything else. Fill coverage gaps. Publish pages that directly answer the tracked questions where you are absent. Make your pages worth citing. Add original data, expert authorship and clear sourcing, and lead with the answer. Build third-party mentions and reviews. These may feed soft mentions and share of voice, and they give models independent evidence about you. Connect visibility to outcomes. Measure visits from AI assistants in your analytics so your reporting goes beyond the score. Visibility is not traffic, and leaders will want to see both. Package a monthly leadership view with the headline score, the component breakdown, the competitor share-of-voice trend, sentiment and next actions. The most persuasive thing you can add to a leadership report is an annotation. A line reading "coverage fell four points after a competitor published a comparison guide; response page scheduled" turns a worrying number into a managed situation. Vendor-specific note: MentionOwl offers a REST API and weekly digests for feeding data into existing dashboards, and cookieless AI traffic analytics for the traffic step above. Other tools offer comparable exports. Whichever you use, avoid maintaining a separate report. Frequently asked questions about AI visibility scores What is a good AI visibility score? There is no universal benchmark. Compare your score with direct competitors on the same questions, platforms and market, and track the trend over several weeks. Why did my AI visibility score drop this week? Identify which component moved, then check for a competitor gain, an engine update or a technical issue. Confirm the change against several weeks of data before treating it as a trend. What is a soft mention? A soft mention is when an AI assistant names your brand without linking to or citing your website. It is usually weighted below a prominent citation. How is AI share of voice different from SEO share of voice? SEO share of voice is typically based on keyword rankings. AI share of voice measures how often your brand is mentioned in generated answers against competitors across a defined question set. How often should I report AI visibility to leadership? Monthly suits most teams, with weekly monitoring for early warnings, because AI answers vary day to day. Putting your AI visibility score into practice A 0-100 figure is a useful summary, but its authority comes from the components beneath it and the consistency of the method behind it. Document your question set, engines, market and counting rules, report the components alongside the headline, and annotate every significant movement. text: On this page An AI visibility score is a 0–100 composite of how often AI engines name your brand, how much of the recommendation space you hold, how early you're named, whether they cite your site, and how they describe you. BugViso's version weights those five parts 35/20/20/15/10. On 280 real unbranded answers, our own brand scored 26.0 and the category leader 39.4 . The weights look arbitrary until you see how each part behaves on real data. By the end of this post you'll be able to recompute the score by hand and spot the two mechanics that make it jump. You'll also know which part to work on first, and you'll have a script that rebuilds the score from your own exported answers. Data used: 35 unbranded buyer prompts × ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Claude × 2 runs on 2026-10-20 (280 answers, web search on), collected by BugViso's AI Visibility Tracker for bugviso.com against five anonymised competitors (A–E). Scores were recomputed offline with the production scoring module. How Do You Measure AI Visibility? To measure AI visibility, fix a set of buyer prompts, ask each one on several AI engines with web search on, and repeat the runs. Count how often your brand is named, cited and ranked against competitors, then combine those counts into one score. Report a range, not a point, because answers vary from run to run. Four choices make that number trustworthy: which prompts you ask (see our guide to building a prompt set ), which engines you query, how many runs you pool ( how often to track AI visibility ), and which competitors you compare against. The rest of this post covers the maths. If you are starting from zero, set up AI visibility tracking first. The AI Visibility Score Formula, Part by Part The score is a weighted sum of five parts, each scaled 0–100: text Copy index = 0.35·V + 0.20·S + 0.20·P + 0.15·C + 0.10·T Part Weight Definition Our brand (pooled) V: Visibility 35 answers that name the brand ÷ successful answers 7.5 S: Share of voice 20 brand appearances ÷ all tracked-brand appearances, once per answer 10.9 P: Position 20 100 × (1 − (avg rank − 1) ÷ (N − 1)), 0 if never named 72.9 C: Citations 15 answers citing the brand's own domain ÷ successful answers 10.7 T: Sentiment 10 mean 0–100 sentiment of answers that name the brand, 0 if never named 50.4 Four rules sit around the formula, and each one changes the result: Unbranded prompts only. A prompt that names you is answered with your name every time. In our data, all 120 branded answers named the brand. Counting them would double the score, as our post on branded vs unbranded prompts shows. Successful answers only. Refusals and empty answers are excluded rather than counted as misses. An engine outage shouldn't look like a visibility drop. Per engine first, then averaged. Each part is computed separately for ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Claude, then averaged with equal weight. An engine that returns more answers doesn't get a bigger vote. N is the size of the tracked set. With you plus five competitors, N = 6. Rank 1 scores 100, rank 6 scores 0, and each step in between is worth 20. These choices follow the usual practice for composite indicators : normalise each part to the same 0–100 scale, then weight them. Fix the rules before you weight anything, because each rule moves the score more than any weight does. Worked Example: Rebuilding 26.0 by Hand Our brand's score of 26.0 comes from five parts, averaged across engines and then weighted. Here are our brand's parts on each engine, computed on 70 unbranded answers per engine: Engine V S P C T Engine index ChatGPT 8.6 15.8 96.7 8.6 63.8 33.2 Gemini 4.3 3.0 100.0 4.3 74.0 30.1 Perplexity 17.1 25.0 95.0 25.7 63.9 40.2 Claude 0.0 0.0 0.0 4.3 0.0 0.6 Average 7.5 10.9 72.9 10.7 50.4 — Plug the averages into the formula: text Copy 0.35 × 7.5 = 2.63 0.20 × 10.9 = 2.18 0.20 × 72.9 = 14.58 0.15 × 10.7 = 1.61 0.10 × 50.4 = 5.04 ----- 26.0 Two things stand out. Position contributes 14.6 of our 26.0 points, more than the other four parts combined. And Claude, the engine that never named us, drags the average down on P and T because both are defined as 0 there. A high P doesn't mean we're winning. Engines named our brand mostly on narrow prompts where it was the obvious answer, and there they named it first. The parts are designed to be read together, never alone. Where the Points Separate Brands The weights tell you what the formula values. The spread tells you what actually decides the ranking. Here's the pooled leaderboard for all six brands: Brand V S P C T Index Competitor A 25.4 24.8 89.1 7.1 66.5 39.4 Competitor B 22.5 19.8 75.7 10.7 55.4 34.1 Competitor E 12.9 11.7 89.7 9.3 65.5 32.7 Competitor C 18.6 18.4 77.5 7.9 55.9 32.5 Competitor D 14.6 14.4 73.3 5.0 64.1 29.8 BugViso 7.5 10.9 72.9 10.7 50.4 26.0 Multiply each part's range across the six brands by its weight and you get how many index points it can separate them by: Part Range across brands × weight Points of separation V 7.5 → 25.4 0.35 6.3 P 72.9 → 89.7 0.20 3.4 S 10.9 → 24.8 0.20 2.8 T 50.4 → 66.5 0.10 1.6 C 5.0 → 10.7 0.15 0.9 Visibility does most of the ranking work, which is the intent: being named at all is what a buyer experiences. Citations separate brands least. Big brands get named without a link to their own site, so their C stays low even when V is high (see when AI names you, does it link your website ). Why Sentiment Gets Only 10% Sentiment is the part people want to weight most and the part that deserves it least. Three reasons, all visible in the data: It barely discriminates. Most brands sit between 55 and 67. Sentiment scorers are calibrated so that 50 means "neutral or merely listed", and most answers just list vendors. It's measured on few answers. T is the mean over answers that name the brand. Our brand had 21. A single critical sentence moves a 21-answer mean by several points. It's conditional on being named. A brand named once, warmly, can out-score one named 70 times in neutral lists. Weighting T heavily would reward being rare. Sentiment still matters as a warning light. A drop below about 40 means answers raise concerns about you, and that belongs in a report whatever the index says. It just shouldn't decide the ranking. Our AI brand sentiment study of 446 scored mentions shows why: a third of single-answer labels flip between runs. The Zero Cliff: How One Mention Moves the Score 6.7 Points The definitions of P and T contain a cliff. On any engine where a brand is never named, both are 0. The first mention lifts P from 0 to as much as 100, and T from 0 to whatever that answer's sentiment is. We simulated one extra first-place mention of our brand (with sentiment 60) on each engine, keeping everything else fixed: Engine that gains one mention Index change ChatGPT (already named 6 times) +0.3 Gemini (already named 3 times) +0.2 Perplexity (already named 12 times) +0.3 Claude (never named) +6.7 One answer out of 280 moves the score by 6.7 points when it lands on a zero engine. The same answer on an engine that already names you is worth 0.3. An extra own-site citation, by comparison, is worth 0.1 wherever it lands. This isn't hypothetical. Competitor D's index rose from 21.2 in the first run to 32.3 in a re-run 23 minutes later. Its ChatGPT mentions went from 0 of 35 answers to 4 of 35, so its ChatGPT index went from 0 to 34.8, and the four-engine average jumped 11 points. Nothing about the brand changed. 💡 Reading rule: when an index moves more than 5 points between runs, check the per-engine table first. A 0 → 1 change on one engine explains most big jumps. How Sensitive Is the Ranking to the Weights? If the weights are a judgement call, the ranking should survive reasonable alternatives. We re-ranked the six brands under four other schemes: Weighting Order (best → worst) Production (35/20/20/15/10) A, B, E, C, D, BugViso Equal (20 each) A, E, B, C, D, BugViso Without sentiment A, B, C, E, D, BugViso Sentiment doubled A, B, E, C, D, BugViso Visibility only A, B, C, D, E, BugViso The top and bottom never move. The middle reshuffles because C and E sit within a point of each other (32.5 vs 32.7). A change that small is inside the run-to-run noise, so a report shouldn't present it as a result. Our brand ranked last under every scheme. That's useful in itself: the score isn't hiding a weak result behind a friendly weighting. Rebuild the Score from Your Own Answers This script recomputes V, S, P and C per engine from a CSV export, averages them across engines and ranks the brands. It also reports what one more first-place mention would be worth on each engine, so you can see where the cliff is. Sentiment needs a language model to score, so the script leaves T out and rescales the other weights, which is what the production scorer does when sentiment can't be measured. python Copy #!/usr/bin/env python3 """AI visibility index (V/S/P/C) per engine and engine-averaged, plus what one more mention is worth. Usage: python3 ai_visibility_index.py answers.csv --brand Acme --domain acme.com \ --competitor Globex --competitor-domain globex.com [--competitor ... --competitor-domain ...] answers.csv columns: engine, answer, cited_urls (space-separated), branded (1/0; branded rows are skipped). Sentiment (T) needs a model, so it is left out and the other weights are rescaled. """ import argparse, csv, re from collections import defaultdict from urllib.parse import urlparse W = {"V": 0.35, "S": 0.20, "P": 0.20, "C": 0.15} def host(u): return (urlparse(u).hostname or "").lower().removeprefix("www.") def parts(answers, brands): """answers: list of (ordered brand list, set of cited hosts).""" n = len(answers) appear, ranks, cites = defaultdict(int), defaultdict(list), defaultdict(int) for order, hosts in answers: for rank, b in enumerate(order, 1): appear[b] += 1; ranks[b].append(rank) for b, d in brands.items(): cites[b] += any(h == d or h.endswith("." + d) for h in hosts) total, N = sum(appear.values()), len(brands) out = {} for b in brands: p = 100 * (1 - (sum(ranks[b]) / len(ranks[b]) - 1) / (N - 1)) if ranks[b] else 0.0 out[b] = {"V": 100 * appear[b] / n, "S": 100 * appear[b] / total if total else 0.0, "P": p, "C": 100 * cites[b] / n} return out def index(p): return sum(W[k] * p[k] for k in W) / sum(W.values()) def main(): ap = argparse.ArgumentParser() ap.add_argument("csv"); ap.add_argument("--brand", required=True); ap.add_argument("--domain", required=True) ap.add_argument("--competitor", action="append", default=[]); ap.add_argument("--competitor-domain", action="append", default=[]) a = ap.parse_args() brands = {a.brand: a.domain.lower(), **{c: d.lower() for c, d in zip(a.competitor, a.competitor_domain)}} rx = {b: re.compile(r"(?<![\w-])" + re.escape(b) + r"(?![\w-])", re.I) for b in brands} by_engine = defaultdict(list) with open(a.csv, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f: for r in csv.DictReader(f): if r.get("branded") == "1" or not r["answer"].strip(): continue # branded prompts name you by construction; empty answers aren't misses hits = {b: m.start() for b, x in rx.items() if (m := x.search(r["answer"]))} by_engine[r["engine"]].append((sorted(hits, key=hits.get), {host(u) for u in r["cited_urls"].split()})) per = {e: parts(ans, brands) for e, ans in sorted(by_engine.items())} avg = {b: {k: sum(per[e][b][k] for e in per) / len(per) for k in W} for b in brands} print(f"{'brand':<16}" + "".join(f"{k:>7}" for k in W) + f"{'index':>8}") for b in sorted(brands, key=lambda b: -index(avg[b])): print(f"{b:<16}" + "".join(f"{avg[b][k]:7.1f}" for k in W) + f"{index(avg[b]):8.1f}") print(f"\nWhat one more {a.brand} mention (first place, own site cited) on each engine is worth:") base = index(avg[a.brand]) for e, ans in by_engine.items(): i = next((i for i, (order, _) in enumerate(ans) if not order), None) if i is None: continue trial = ans[:i] + [([a.brand], {brands[a.brand]})] + ans[i + 1:] p = dict(per); p[e] = parts(trial, brands) new = {k: sum(p[x][a.brand][k] for x in p) / len(p) for k in W} print(f" {e:<11} {index(new) - base:+.1f} points") if __name__ == "__main__": main() bash Copy python3 ai_visibility_index.py answers.csv --brand "Acme" --domain acme.com \ --competitor "Globex" --competitor-domain globex.com \ --competitor "Initech" --competitor-domain initech.io On our 280 answers it reproduces the production V, S, P and C exactly (7.5, 10.9, 72.9, 10.7). Without sentiment, our index comes out at 23.3 and the Claude cliff at +5.8 . Exact-name matching is deliberately simple; add aliases and domains as described in our brand mention detection guide . How BugViso Computes the Score BugViso's AI Visibility Tracker computes the score after every run. It asks each prompt on ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Claude and Google AI Overviews with web search on (for example OpenAI's web search tool and Gemini's grounding with Google Search ), then applies the formula above to the unbranded answers, engine by engine. The AI visibility score you see is the engine average, with the same five parts listed underneath so you can see which one moved. The same computation also produces: A leaderboard that ranks you against at least three competitors. Ties share a rank and visibility breaks them. An engine scorecard with mention rate, prompt coverage, citation coverage, share of voice and accuracy for each engine, which is where a zero engine shows up first. Segments by engine, buyer stage and topic. Any segment built on fewer than 20 answers is flagged low confidence. A 95% Wilson score interval on visibility. Ours was 5.0–11.2% around a 7.5% point estimate. Score drivers. Each part's points and how far it moved since the comparison run. AI Overviews joins the average only once Google has shown an overview on at least five unbranded queries. Otherwise one engine with three answers would weigh as much as one with seventy. Removing a wrong mention recomputes the run's score from the stored answers. The full breakdown is on the AI visibility tracker page. Five Mistakes When Reading the Number Comparing scores across competitor sets. S and P both depend on who else is tracked. A score against three competitors can't be compared with one against five. Treating P as good news. High position with low visibility means "named first on the few prompts where you're named", not "leading". Our AI answer position ranking analysis shows how far solo mentions inflate it. Ignoring the per-engine table. An 11-point jump can be one engine going from zero to one mention, as Competitor D's did. Mixing in branded prompts. It inflates every part at once. Keep branded answers for accuracy and sentiment checks. Calling a one-point gap a lead. Competitors C and E differ by 0.2. Our two runs differed by 0.9 on the same prompts. For the sample sizes behind a stable number, see how often to track AI visibility . Frequently Asked Questions What is a good AI visibility score? There's no universal benchmark for an AI visibility score, because the score depends on your competitor list and prompts. Compare yourself with the leader on the same prompts, engines and competitor set. In our category, the leader scored 39.4 and the last of six brands 26.0. How is an AI visibility score calculated? Compute five parts per engine on unbranded answers: visibility, share of voice, position, own-site citations and sentiment. Average each part across engines, then weight them 35/20/20/15/10 and add them up. Why did my AI visibility score jump overnight? Usually because one engine went from never naming you to naming you once, which lifts both position and sentiment from zero. Check the per-engine parts before you celebrate. Should sentiment count more in an AI visibility score? Not for ranking. Sentiment varies little between brands, it's measured only on answers that name you, and it can reward brands that are rarely named. Track it separately as a warning signal. Does an AI visibility score include Google AI Overviews? In BugViso, yes, once Google has shown an overview for at least five unbranded queries in the run. Until then, AI Overviews is reported on its own and kept out of the average. Related Guides on AI Visibility Tracking The score is the summary. text: Quick answer An AI visibility score is a single number, usually on a 0 to 100 scale, showing how often and how favorably your brand appears in AI-generated answers. It rolls up mention rate, citation rate, share of voice, average position and sentiment. To check yours, run high-intent prompts across AI platforms against chosen competitors, or use a tracker like Erlin to get an instant baseline. According to Erlin's 2026 State of AI Search report , 67% of marketing leaders don't know how to measure their AI visibility, and 58% say no one on their team owns it. Meanwhile, AI-referred visitors tend to convert better than traditional organic visitors, so this is a channel worth measuring properly. Every month without a baseline is a month of guessing. This article explains what an AI visibility score is, how it's calculated, what affects it, and how to check yours. What is an AI visibility score? An AI visibility score is a composite metric that measures how consistently and favorably your brand appears in AI-generated answers. When someone asks Perplexity, "Compare HubSpot vs Salesforce," the AI system pulls from a pool of sources and returns a small set of brands, usually two to four. Whether your brand makes that list, how often it does, and how it's described is what the AI visibility score tracks. Unlike SEO rankings, which operate on a spectrum, AI visibility is closer to binary per query: you're either in the answer or you're not. Brands with high scores show up consistently. Brands with low scores appear occasionally or not at all. What an AI visibility score looks like in practice The screenshot below from Erlin's dashboard makes this concrete. The metrics across the top give you your headline numbers at a glance: Mention Rate (8.4%), Citation Rate (0.0%), Share of Voice (8.4%), Average Position (4.4), and Sentiment (70). The AI Visibility Score chart shows the brand sitting at 25.0% over a week-long window, meaning it appeared in about one in four relevant AI-generated answers. That's your baseline. The "AI vs Other Traffic" panel shows where sessions are actually coming from, and the Platform Breakdown table splits performance by platform: ChatGPT at 13.7% mention rate and 4.9 average position, Perplexity at 3.3% and 3.0. What's useful about this view is how little you need to interpret. If your mention rate is 8% and a competitor's is 22%, you know where you stand. The score doesn't explain why, that's what the platform's opportunity analysis is for, but it tells you clearly that there's a gap worth closing. The metrics that matter now The AI visibility score is an aggregate, which means it's worth understanding what goes into it. These are the individual metrics that matter in 2026. Mention rate tracks how often your brand appears by name in AI-generated answers. If you run 100 relevant queries and your brand shows up in 8 of the responses, your mention rate is 8%. It's the clearest signal of raw presence. Citation rate is narrower: it measures how often AI platforms link out to or explicitly source your content. A mention means the AI named you. A citation means it's treating your content as a reference. Citation rate tends to be lower, and it's often what separates brands that get traffic from AI search versus brands that just get mentioned. Share of voice puts your numbers in a competitive context. The formula is simple: your mentions divided by total industry mentions times 100. If your brand is mentioned 18 times across 100 relevant responses and competitors are mentioned a combined 82 times, your AI share of voice is 18%. This is arguably the most actionable metric because it tells you not just where you are, but who's winning the space you're competing for. Average position tracks where in the AI response your brand typically appears. First mention carries more weight than being buried in a list of six. Some tracking tools weight this into the overall score; others report it separately. Sentiment score captures how AI describes your brand when it does mention you. A brand mentioned frequently but described as "expensive" or "limited" has a different challenge than one with positive, specific framing. Sentiment gaps often reveal content or reputation issues that raw mention counts don't surface. Together, these five metrics paint a complete picture of AI search performance. Tracking one in isolation gives you an incomplete view. How the AI visibility score is measured AI visibility trackers operate like rank trackers but for generative AI. These trackers query LLMs with relevant prompts to detect brand appearances. Here’s how the process looks like: Define target prompts based on user intents (e.g., "best [product] for [use case]") grouped by topics or buyer stages. Run prompts repeatedly across AI platforms (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Copilot) to capture variability in responses. Analyze responses for metrics like mention frequency, position, citations, sentiment, and query breadth. Normalize and weight components into a composite score (often 0-100), then benchmark against competitors for share of voice. Update daily or weekly. Filter hallucinations via cross-validation and track trends over time. Common score components Most trackers use weighted factors normalized per industry.​ Component Weight Example Description Mention Frequency 40% How often the brand appears across queries, adjusted for response length.​ Position & Prominence 25% Placement (e.g., top recommendation scores higher than footnotes).​ Citation Quality 20% Authority of sources cited (e.g., official sites over forums).​ Query Coverage 15% Breadth across diverse prompts and intents.​ A tool like Erlin runs thousands of purchase-intent prompts across ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, Google AI Mode, Gemini, and Copilot. For each prompt, it captures: which brands were mentioned, in what order, with what framing, and whether content was linked or cited. That raw data gets aggregated into scores for each metric, then rolled up into the overall AI visibility score. The score itself is typically expressed on a 0 to 100 scale. Erlin's research defines the maturity tiers this way: AI Invisible (under 20%): minimal appearance in AI answers; limited structured data and weak citation signals AI Fragile (20 to 40%): inconsistent inclusion, concentrated in a narrow set of queries AI Present (40 to 60%): regular appearance in core category queries; structured content in place AI Preferred (60 to 80%): consistent inclusion in high-intent and comparison queries; strong authority signals AI Dominant (80%+): frequent top inclusion across core and adjacent categories; sustained citation authority Most brands that have never optimized for AI search land in the Invisible or Fragile tier. The prompt library matters as much as the measurement itself. Erlin's platform suggests high-intent prompts relevant to your category: queries that mirror what buyers actually type when they're in research mode, not generic brand awareness questions. Factors that affect your AI visibility score Content quality and fact density AI systems don't evaluate brand holistically. They evaluate specific factual claims they can extract, verify, and reuse in an answer. Erlin's analysis of 500+ brands found that brands with 9+ structured facts in their content coverage (pricing, features, use cases, technical specs, comparison data) achieve 78% AI coverage. Brands with 0 to 2 facts achieve just 9%. Marketing language doesn't help. Claims like "industry-leading platform" or "the most innovative solution" give AI nothing to work with. Specific, extractable facts, such as integration counts, pricing tiers, setup time, customer outcomes, etc., are what get cited. Entity coverage and clarity AI systems need to understand who you are before they can recommend you. Entity coverage refers to how clearly and consistently your brand identity is defined across the web: your website, Wikipedia, third-party reviews, press mentions, and social profiles. Inconsistent or incomplete signals lead to omission. This is different from SEO. You don't need the most backlinks. You need the clearest signal. Erlin's data found that smaller brands with strong entity context routinely outperform Fortune 500 companies in specific query categories. AI doesn't default to the biggest brand. It defaults to the clearest one. Structured data and technical signals How your content is formatted affects whether AI can read it at all. Erlin's research shows that static HTML with schema markup achieves a 94% AI parsing success rate. JavaScript-rendered content drops to 23%. PDFs land at 7%. Three specific formats show consistent coverage lifts: comparison tables (about 34% higher coverage within two weeks), llm.txt files (32% lift), and FAQ schema markup (28% lift over three weeks). These aren't cosmetic improvements; they directly affect whether AI can extract your content as a citable source. Citation history and momentum Third-party validation is the biggest lever most brands aren't using. Erlin's research found that third-party sources drive 68% of all AI citations. Reddit discussions carry a 3.4x citation lift over owned content alone. Wikipedia articles carry 2.9x. Review platforms and affiliates come in at 2.6x. Your own website content is the baseline. Third-party validation is what separates brands that appear occasionally from brands that appear consistently. Content freshness AI systems continuously re-evaluate brand information for recency. Brands that update content monthly maintain roughly 23% higher AI representation than those that don't. Content under 3 months old has 48% average coverage. Content older than 24 months drops to 18%. The staleness penalty is estimated at about 1.8% AI coverage per month of inactivity. That's not catastrophic month to month, but it compounds. Competitive landscape AI typically cites 2 to 3 brands per response, which creates a winner-take-most dynamic. Your score isn't static. It shifts as competitors improve their visibility. Monitoring share of voice against specific competitors matters because a rising competitor in your category can suppress your appearances even if your absolute content quality hasn't changed. How to check your brand's AI visibility score The process is quicker than you'd think. Here's how it works using Erlin, one of the few tools that ties visibility tracking directly to content action, rather than just monitoring. Step 1: pick your tracking platform Look for a tool that covers multiple AI platforms at once, supports competitor benchmarking, integrates with GA/GSC, and includes a prompt library for your category. For teams that want to move from "here's where I'm falling short" to "here's how to fix it" without jumping between tools, Erlin is built exactly for that. The gap analysis flows straight into an action center. Step 2: sign up and add your domain Head to app.erlin.ai/get-started . Once you enter your domain, Erlin automatically pulls brand context, gathers social signals, and builds baseline insights in the background. No manual configuration needed. Step 3: add your competitors Erlin recommends up to five competitors based on your domain and category. Keep the suggestions, replace them, or add your own. Your AI visibility score is most useful in context: knowing you're at 25% hits differently when your closest competitor is sitting at 61%. Step 4: select the prompts you want to track Erlin surfaces high-intent prompts relevant to your category; the kinds of queries buyers actually use when they're actively researching. You can refine the list, add industry-specific terms, or zero in on the prompts where beating competitors matters most. Step 5: review your baseline snapshot Once setup is complete, you get an instant read: your AI Visibility Score, Traffic Rank, and a side-by-side competitor comparison. The dashboard breaks down platform-level data by mention rate, citation rate, and average position across AI platforms like ChatGPT and Perplexity. The "AI vs Other Traffic" panel tracks how AI referral traffic stacks up against traditional sessions over time. The "AI vs Other Conversion Rate" panel tends to be where eyebrows go up. For many brands, AI traffic converts well above other channels, which is why this panel is worth watching. This is your baseline. Every future change, whether it's a content update, schema fix, or citation campaign, gets measured against it. How to improve your AI visibility score 1. Audit your current AI presence Before optimizing anything, understand what AI is already saying about your brand. In Erlin, checking your AI visibility shows how AI platforms currently describe your brand, what they get wrong, and where you're absent from conversations where competitors appear. Run the brand audit checklist from Erlin's report on: Fact density (pricing accessible? features in scannable formats? competitive positioning explicit?) Third-party validation (reviews on major platforms? Reddit presence? Wikipedia mentions?) Structured data (llm.txt file? FAQ schema? schema.org markup?) Each "no" is a concrete gap with an estimated coverage impact. 2. Identify citation gaps Pull your competitor comparison data and look for specific prompts where competitors appear and you don't. Those are your highest-priority gaps: the queries where buyer intent is high, and you're currently invisible. Citation gaps usually fall into two buckets: content gaps (you don't have content that addresses this query) and structural gaps (you have content, but AI can't parse or surface it). They require different fixes. 3. Create entity-rich content Rewrite key pages around extractable facts. Every page where AI might pull a response should have: specific pricing or pricing ranges, clear feature descriptions with technical details, use cases tied to real scenarios, and comparison information that makes your differentiation explicit. If your homepage says "powerful, flexible platform," that's not extractable. If it says "integrates with 200+ tools, setup under 30 minutes, used by 5,000+ teams," that is. 4. Optimize technical signals Implement FAQ schema on question-based pages. Add an llm.txt file that summarizes your brand's key facts in a format AI crawlers can read easily. Make sure your most important content, pricing, features, comparison pages, is available in static HTML, not JavaScript-rendered. Check that schema.org Product or Organization markup is in place on key pages. Erlin's data suggests that addressing all five structural signals moves brands from 23 to 35% coverage to 60 to 80% coverage. That's not a marginal improvement. 5. Build authoritative third-party validation This takes longer than the technical fixes, but it has the highest impact. Pursue verified reviews on G2, Capterra, and industry platforms. Get into relevant Reddit discussions, not promotional, genuinely helpful answers to questions in your category. Aim for coverage in industry publications and blogs that AI systems treat as authoritative sources. Erlin tracks citation shifts across third-party sources and alerts teams when brand mentions or AI citation positions change, so you can see the impact of this work in near-real-time rather than waiting for quarterly reviews. 6. Monitor and iterate AI visibility decays without maintenance. Brands that go silent lose roughly 1.8% AI coverage per month. Monitored brands catch errors in about 14 days; unmonitored brands take an average of 67 days, by which point the damage is compounding. Erlin's platform runs continuous prompt tracking and flags when citation positions shift, content goes stale, or a competitor surges. That's the difference between managing AI visibility as a channel and discovering six months later that you've lost ground you can't easily recover.

title: Visibility Score and metric formulas - RankRaft AI Docs
text: Every number in RankRaft AI is calculated from the stored answers in the selected date range. Nothing is modelled or estimated. Every rate counts only answers that were actually shown: when Google shows no AI Overview for a question, that run is left out rather than counted as “not mentioned”. ​ Visibility Score A single number from 0 to 100: Score = 100 × ( 0.45 M + 0.35 C + 0.20 P ) \text{Score} = 100 \times (0.45\,M + 0.35\,C + 0.20\,P) Score = 100 × ( 0.45 M + 0.35 C + 0.20 P ) where M is your mention rate, C your citation rate and P your prompt coverage, each between 0 and 1. The result is rounded to the nearest whole number. Component Weight Why Mention rate 45% Being named is the outcome that matters most. Citation rate 35% A link is evidence AI trusts your site, and it’s what sends traffic. Prompt coverage 20% Rewards showing up across many questions rather than dominating one. Position isn’t part of the score on purpose. It’s only defined for answers that list brands in order, so including it would penalise brands mentioned in prose. ​ Component metrics Metric Formula Mention rate answers that name you (or an alias) ÷ all answers Citation rate answers that link to at least one page on your domain ÷ all answers Prompt coverage prompts where you were named at least once ÷ prompts asked in the range Average spot in each answer, the brands found are numbered by first appearance (1 = named first). Averaged over answers that mention you, to one decimal place Share of voice your mentions ÷ all brand mentions, counting you and every competitor on your list, confirmed or not. Each brand counts once per answer ​ Example In a week with 10 prompts on 3 engines (210 answers): you’re named in 63 answers, cited in 21, and named at least once for 6 of the 10 prompts. Mention rate = 63 ÷ 210 = 30% Citation rate = 21 ÷ 210 = 10% Prompt coverage = 6 ÷ 10 = 60% Visibility Score = 100 × (0.45 × 0.30 + 0.35 × 0.10 + 0.20 × 0.60) = 29 ​ Margin Every score carries a 95% interval, shown as ± N and as a shaded band on trend charts: margin = 100 × 1.96 × p ( 1 − p ) n \text{margin} = 100 \times 1.96 \times \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} margin = 100 × 1.96 × n p ( 1 − p ) ​ ​ where p is your mention rate (held between 5% and 95%) and n is the number of answers. The margin is never shown as less than 1 point. More prompts, more engines and longer date ranges all narrow it. Tied within margin: on the leaderboard, two neighbouring brands whose scores differ by no more than their combined margins are marked as tied. Don’t read anything into the order of tied brands. ​ Competitors Competitors are scored with exactly the same formula, over the same answers. A competitor is cited when an answer links to its domain or a subdomain of it. Rank orders you and your confirmed competitors by Visibility Score. ​ Importance Prompts and gap prompts are tagged by importance, based on your mention rate for that prompt: Importance Your mention rate High 0% Medium Below 40% Low 40% or more ​ Small samples Figures based on very few answers are greyed out and labelled Low sample · N answers . Treat them as a hint, not a result. ​ Why past numbers can change The scores for a date range are recalculated from the stored answers whenever you look. They change if you: Confirm or archive a competitor. The leaderboard and rank show confirmed competitors only, so confirming one adds its row, with its full history, and archiving one removes it. Share of voice doesn’t move: every competitor’s mentions are always in the total, whether or not its row is shown. - Change the range. A 30-day score covers different answers from a 7-day score. Adding a competitor yourself, or a new alias, works differently: brand names are matched when each answer is collected, so the change counts from the next scan onward. Earlier answers keep the matches made at the time. Was this page helpful? Yes No
